summary: Ohio is known as the Buckeye State. But what exactly is a buckeye?
body_html: The buckeye tree (Aesculus glabra) became Ohio’s official state tree in 1953. Native to North America, it produces shiny brown nuts with a light spot—looking like a deer’s eye, which is how the tree got its name. Since the mid-1800s, “Buckeye” has been a nickname for Ohioans. It became popular during William Henry Harrison’s presidential campaign, when supporters made souvenirs from buckeye wood. The name appears all over the state—in places like Buckeye Lake, the Buckeye Trail, and the town of Buckeye in Jackson County. Many Ohio businesses and groups also use the name. The Ohio State University’s mascot is the Buckeye, and students and alumni proudly call themselves Buckeyes. The name even inspired a sweet treat: chocolate buckeyes. These peanut butter candies are dipped in chocolate to look like the nut—but unlike the real nut, the candy is safe (and delicious) to eat!

title: Close a Business
summary: Follow these steps to officially close your business in Ohio.
body_html: To officially close your business with the State of Ohio, you may need to take several steps, including filing a dissolution with the Secretary of State and closing any state-level business accounts. Additional steps may be required at the federal and local levels. Depending on your business structure, you may need to file a formal dissolution with the Ohio Secretary of State to legally end your business entity.  How to Dissolve a Business You must cancel all business accounts registered with the state and terminate any active licenses. Below are common accounts and filings that may need to be closed: You must close your tax accounts, which may include filing a final sales tax return and canceling your vendor’s license. You may also need to close: Domestic, for-profit corporations must also obtain a Certificate of Tax Clearance. Contact the Department of Taxation Deactivate your unemployment online in The SOURCE, Ohio's unemployment insurance tax system. Contact the Ohio Department of Job and Family Services. You must cancel your workers' compensation policy with the Ohio Bureau of Workers' Compensation. Failure to do so may result in continued billing, penalties, and invoices.  Contact BWC. If your business or profession required a license, you may need to cancel it. For general information and contacts, visit the Licenses & Permits page.

title: Volunteer Opportunities
summary: More than three million Ohioans give their time and talents to their communities and state each year.
body_html:
Ohio is the heart of service. Let us show you the many volunteer opportunities that Ohio government programs and agencies offer. The Adopt-A-Highway program uses volunteers to control litter on Ohio highways while saving taxpayers money. 
The Ohio Department of Transportation (ODOT) recruits groups to adopt a two-mile section or an interchange along a state, federal or interstate route. It costs the group nothing - ODOT provides the supplies and training - and their participation is recognized on prominent road signs along their route. The Ohio Children’s Trust Fund uses volunteers to help build strong communities, healthy families, and safe children. They focus on parents, caregivers, and professionals who serve families.  Make Me a Firefighter is a national campaign to connect local fire departments and emergency medical services with individuals who want to make a difference, protect property, and save lives. Ohio is proud to support efforts to recruit the volunteer firefighters, EMTs, and other first responders our communities desperately need. Long-Term Care Ombudsman volunteers step up for long-term care consumers who are living in their own homes, in nursing homes, or in assisted living facilities. They visit, observe, and talk to residents. When volunteers discover problems or concerns about care and services, they work with the full Ombudsman team, the resident, the resident's family, and facility staff to resolve them.  The Ohio Military Reserve helps state and local governments prepare for, respond to, and communicate during emergencies. They also support the work of the Ohio Adjutant General's Department and the Ohio National Guard.  Volunteers with the Ohio Department of Natural Resources engage in a variety of activities, from maintaining state parks and helping campers, to teaching hunters and boaters, to conservation programs and more. On Election Day, thousands of Ohioans volunteer as poll workers and help operate neighborhood polling places. The Department of Rehabilitation and Correction uses volunteers and reentry mentors to improve the quality of life in Ohio prisons and help prepare incarcerated individuals to return to their communities. Volunteers help with rehabilitation and reentry efforts. Time and experience make older adults a great resource for Ohio communities. The Department of Aging partners with other state entities to provide unique volunteer opportunities that appeal to people with many different interests and abilities. Your local senior center or community action agency may also welcome volunteers for a variety of programs.  ServeOhio engages AmeriCorps members and community volunteers to help their communities in key ways. They use volunteers to address issues in education, health, the economy, and the environment, among others. You can use their Get Connected platform to find volunteer opportunities that match your interests.  Ohio has a rich history and a robust government. Volunteers help residents and visitors learn about the people and places that shaped our state. Ohio Statehouse Volunteers lead group tours in the center of Ohio Government. Ohio Supreme Court Volunteers support the court's visitor education center with tours of the court building. Ohio Governor's Residence Volunteers teach visitors about the governor's home and heritage gardens. Ohio History Connection Volunteers support events and historical sites. The Ohio Veterans Homes use volunteers from local schools, hospitals, veterans organizations, and community groups to foster education and community service at the state's nursing facilities exclusively for veterans. Learn how to volunteer from the Ohio Department of Veteran Services. The Ohio Department of Youth Services recruits volunteers to mentor and help youth within their facilities. Volunteers help ensure these children, teens. and young adults have the skills they'll need for a successful and crime-free future.

title: Ohio Facts: State Symbols
summary: Explore the many symbols that represent our great state.
body_html:
Since the early 1800s, Ohio lawmakers have chosen symbols to honor the state’s people, places, and history. Most of these symbols are listed in Chapter 5 of the Ohio Revised Code, while others were created through special resolutions passed by the legislature. Ohio’s state flag is called the Ohio burgee. It was designed by John Eisenmann in 1901 and became the official state flag in 1902. Unlike most state flags, it has a swallowtail shape, which makes it unique. The flag has: The flag’s design is described in Ohio Revised Code, Section 5.01. Rules for displaying and caring for the flag are in Ohio Revised Code, Section 5.012. Ohio’s coat of arms shows a sunrise over Mount Logan, with the Scioto River and a farm field in the foreground. On the left is a sheaf of wheat, and on the right is a bundle of 17 arrows, representing Ohio as the 17th state. The design is described in Ohio Revised Code, Section 5.04. The Great Seal of the State of Ohio includes the coat of arms inside a circle with the words “THE GREAT SEAL OF THE STATE OF OHIO.” The current design was adopted in 1996. The seal is used by state officials, courts, and some agencies. Others must get permission from the Governor’s Office to use it. Rules for the seal’s design and use are in Ohio Revised Code, section 5.10. Ohio’s state motto is “With God, All Things Are Possible.” It was suggested in 1958 by James Mastronardo, a 10-year-old from Cincinnati. With help from his state senator, he gathered signatures and spoke to lawmakers to support the idea. The motto became official in October 1959.  The phrase, a favorite of his mother, is from the Bible—Matthew 19:26. While it comes from a religious text, it’s meant to express hope and determination, not to promote a specific religion. The motto is defined in Ohio Revised Code, section 5.06. Ohio’s official slogan is “Ohio, The Heart of it All.” It highlights Ohio’s central location and its strong sense of community. The slogan is used to promote tourism and to show that Ohio is a great place to live, learn, work, and raise a family. State agencies and organizations also use the slogan to share what makes Ohio special. It’s part of the state’s official branding for visitors and residents alike Columbus is Ohio’s capital city. It's located in Franklin county, near the center of the state. The Ohio Statehouse, found in downtown Columbus, is where the state’s government meets. It has: The Statehouse is not just a government building—it’s also a historic site and a symbol of Ohio’s democracy. Ohio is known as the Buckeye state. People from Ohio are often called Buckeyes, a nickname that dates back to the early 1800s. The name comes from the buckeye tree, which grows across the state. Its nut looks like a deer’s eye—dark brown with a light spot—and early settlers thought it was a good symbol for Ohio. The nickname became popular during William Henry Harrison’s presidential campaign in 1840. His supporters made souvenirs from buckeye wood, helping the name stick. Today, “Buckeye” is used all over Ohio. For example, you'll find it: What started as a simple nickname is now a proud symbol of Ohio’s identity. The Ohio Legislature can create special days, weeks, or months to raise awareness about important people, events, or causes. These observances are listed in Chapter 5 of the Ohio Revised Code, along with the state’s official symbols. Some examples include: These observances help educate the public and honor Ohio’s history, health, and community. Adopted: 1953 The cardinal is Ohio’s official state bird. It’s a small songbird that stays in Ohio all year. Cardinals are easy to spot: Cardinals eat seeds, fruits, and insects. They are known for being territorial and often mate for life. The state bird is defined in Ohio Revised Code, section 5.06. Adopted: 1975 The ladybug, also called the ladybird beetle, is Ohio’s official state insect. It’s a small, shiny red bug with black spots, active from spring through fall. Ladybugs are harmless to people but very helpful to farmers and gardeners. They eat aphids and other bugs that damage plants. The most common type in Ohio is the seven-spotted ladybug. It has: Their bright colors and bad taste help protect them from predators. Adopted: 1988 The white-tailed deer has lived in Ohio since the last Ice Age. It has a gray-brown coat and gets its name from the white underside of its tail, which it raises when alarmed. Native peoples used deer for food, clothing, and tools. Early settlers traded deerskins for supplies, which is how the word “buck” came to mean money. White-tailed deer are foragers. They eat grasses, nuts, berries, wildflowers, crops, and woody plants. Because of their diet, they’re often found near forests and neighborhoods Adopted: 1995 The black racer lives mostly in the eastern and southern parts of the state. This snake is: Black racers are helpful to farmers and gardeners because they eat rodents and other small pests. While they can act aggressive if they feel threatened, their bite is not poisonous—just painful. Adopted: 2010 The spotted salamander lives in moist woodlands near ponds, swamps, and creeks. These salamanders are: They eat insects, earthworms, small amphibians, and even tiny mice. Because they’re hard to spot, seeing one in the wild is a special treat! Adopted: 2010 The bullfrog is the largest frog in North America. It lives in ponds, marshes, and slow-moving streams across the state. Bullfrogs are: They are solitary and territorial. They eat crayfish, insects, mice, and even other frogs. Bullfrogs can live for 7 to 9 years and are most active from late April through summer. Adopted: 2019 Ohio named the shelter pet as its official state pet to help raise awareness about the many cats and dogs waiting for homes in shelters across the state. Each year, about 6.5 million animals enter shelters in the U.S., but only half are adopted. By choosing a shelter pet, you’re giving an animal a second chance at life. To adopt, contact your local animal shelter or humane society and learn how you can help a pet find a loving home. Adopted: 1953 The scarlet carnation is a colorful plant with fringed petals and a spicy scent. The flower is popular in bouquets and can grow up to 2.5 feet tall. The red carnation stands for love and passion. It was a favorite of President William McKinley, who was born in Ohio and often wore one on his jacket.  Adopted: 1953 The buckeye tree is native to North America. In late summer and early fall, it produces a nut that’s dark brown with a light spot, resembling a deer’s eye—which is how the tree got its name. The nut also inspired the popular chocolate buckeye candy. These treats are made of peanut butter dipped in chocolate, with a bit of the lighter-colored filling left showing to look like the real nut. While the buckeye nut is poisonous, the candy version is safe and delicious Adopted: 1987 The white trillium grows in all 88 Ohio counties and blooms in the spring with a large, white flower made of three petals. Also called the wake robin or snow trillium, this plant grows best in shady woodlands. Native Americans once used its leaves for food and roots for medicine. Adopted: 2009 Many experts credit Alexander W. Livingston, an Ohio native, with creating the modern tomato. In 1870, he developed the “Paragon” tomato, which was larger and sweeter than most tomatoes at the time. Livingston went on to grow tomatoes commercially and created more than 30 varieties. By the late 1800s, tomato farming had become a big part of Ohio’s agriculture—and it still is today. Adopted: 2009 The pawpaw is the only edible fruit native to Ohio. Native Americans in the Ohio Valley used it for food and trade as early as the 1500s. Pawpaws are: They taste like a mix of banana and mango and are packed with protein, vitamin C, iron, and potassium. The best time to pick pawpaws is in mid-September. Adopted: 1965 In 1870, Ohioan Alexander W. Livingston created the modern tomato with his sweet and juicy “Paragon” variety. His tomatoes helped make tomato juice a popular and healthy drink. Tomato juice is: Due to its popularity, tomatoes and tomato juice are big parts of Ohio’s farming and food industry. Adopted: 1989 The music for “Beautiful Ohio” was written by Mary Earl, and the original lyrics were by Ballard MacDonald. In 1989, Wilbert B. McBride updated the lyrics to better reflect Ohio’s cities, industries, and farmland. The song celebrates Ohio’s beauty and strength. Here’s the chorus: Beautiful Ohio, where the golden grain
Dwarfs the lovely flowers in the summer rain.
Cities rising high, silhouette the sky.
Freedom is supreme in this majestic land;
Mighty factories seem to hum in tune, so grand.
Beautiful Ohio, thy wonders are in view,
Land where my dreams all come true! Adopted: 1985 Ohio is the only state with an official rock song—“Hang on Sloopy.” It became a hit in 1965 when it was recorded by The McCoys, a band with Ohio roots. Two members, Randy and Rick Derringer, were from the state. The song is believed to be about Dorothy Sloop, a singer from Steubenville, Ohio, who used the nickname Sloopy. The Ohio State University Marching Band first played the song at a football game in October 1965. The version arranged by John Tagenhorst became a fan favorite and is still played at games today. It’s now a proud part of Ohio’s music and sports culture. Adopted: 2002 The Blaine Hill Bridge is the oldest and longest sandstone bridge in Ohio. It was built in 1826 and crosses Wheeling Creek in Belmont County. The bridge has a unique three-arch “S” shape and was part of the National Road Project, which helped connect the country in the 1800s. It closed to traffic in 1994, but local efforts saved it from being torn down. In 1999, the Blaine Bridge Community Preservation Project began restoring the bridge. It was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2010. Adopted: 2006 Long ago, ancient people in what is now Ohio built huge shapes and structures out of earth. These were made by the Hopewell culture between 1 and 400 A.D. The Newark Earthworks is the largest of these sites. It once covered over 4 square miles and used more than 7 million cubic feet of soil. The site was likely used as a ceremonial center, a burial ground, and even an astronomical observatory. Today, three major parts of the earthworks still remain: These earthworks are a powerful reminder of Ohio’s ancient history and are now protected as a World Heritage Site. Adopted: 2013 The Adena Pipe is one of Ohio’s most famous ancient artifacts. It was found in 1901 in a burial mound near Chillicothe, on the estate of Thomas Worthington, Ohio’s 6th governor. The pipe is carved from Ohio pipestone and shaped like a man wearing a loincloth and feather bustle. It was likely used for ceremonial tobacco smoking and may have belonged to a leader or spiritual figure. The Adena culture, which built the mound, lived in the Scioto and Hocking River valleys from about 800 B.C. to 100 A.D.  Adopted: 2019 Barns are a big part of Ohio’s farming history. You can find them all over the state—from Lake Erie to the Ohio River. These buildings come in many shapes, sizes, and colors, depending on the needs of the farm and the style of the builder. Some barns were even painted with murals or ads. From 1997 to 2002, artist Scott Hagan painted a barn in each of Ohio’s 88 counties with a special logo to celebrate Ohio’s 200th birthday in 2003. Barns remind us of Ohio’s strong agricultural roots and the people who helped build its communities. Adopted: 2025 In 1905, Ohio inventors Wilbur and Orville Wright built the Wright Flyer III. It was their strongest and most reliable airplane yet. On June 23, 1905, Orville Wright made the first flight with it. By October, the plane flew 25 miles—a huge improvement over earlier flights. It was also the first airplane to carry a passenger, marking a major moment in aviation history. Adopted: 1965 Flint is a tough, glassy rock that was very important to Native Americans in Ohio. A type of quartz, it breaks into sharp edges, making it perfect for tools and weapons.Early settlers also used it for starting fires, flintlock guns, and grinding tools.  The best source in the state was Flint Ridge, located in Licking and Muskingum counties. People came from hundreds of miles away to gather flint there.  Today, flint is often polished and worn as jewelry. body_text: Since the early 1800s, Ohio lawmakers have chosen symbols to honor the state’s people, places, and history. Most of these symbols are listed in Chapter 5 of the Ohio Revised Code , while others were created through special resolutions passed by the legislature. State Flag Ohio’s state flag is called the Ohio burgee . It was designed by John Eisenmann in 1901 and became the official state flag in 1902. Unlike most state flags, it has a swallowtail shape, which makes it unique. The flag has: Five stripes (three red and two white) for Ohio’s roads and rivers, A blue triangle that stands for the state’s hills and valleys. Seventeen white stars to show that Ohio was the 17th state to join the U.S., and A red circle with a white border in the center, which looks like an “O” for Ohio and also represents the state’s nickname, the Buckeye State. The flag’s design is described in Ohio Revised Code, Section 5.01 . Rules for displaying and caring for the flag are in Ohio Revised Code, Section 5.012 . Coat of Arms and State Seal Ohio’s coat of arms shows a sunrise over Mount Logan , with the Scioto River and a farm field in the foreground. On the left is a sheaf of wheat, and on the right is a bundle of 17 arrows, representing Ohio as the 17th state. The design is described in Ohio Revised Code, Section 5.04 . The Great Seal of the State of Ohio includes the coat of arms inside a circle with the words “THE GREAT SEAL OF THE STATE OF OHIO.” The current design was adopted in 1996. The seal is used by state officials, courts, and some agencies. Others must get permission from the Governor’s Office to use it. Rules for the seal’s design and use are in Ohio Revised Code, section 5.10 . State Motto Ohio’s state motto is “With God, All Things Are Possible.” It was suggested in 1958 by James Mastronardo , a 10-year-old from Cincinnati. With help from his state senator, he gathered signatures and spoke to lawmakers to support the idea. The motto became official in October 1959. The phrase, a favorite of his mother, is from the Bible—Matthew 19:26. While it comes from a religious text, it’s meant to express hope and determination, not to promote a specific religion. The motto is defined in Ohio Revised Code, section 5.06 . State Slogan Ohio’s official slogan is “Ohio, The Heart of it All.” It highlights Ohio’s central location and its strong sense of community. The slogan is used to promote tourism and to show that Ohio is a great place to live, learn, work, and raise a family. State agencies and organizations also use the slogan to share what makes Ohio special. It’s part of the state’s official branding for visitors and residents alike State Capital and Capitol Building Columbus is Ohio’s capital city . It's located in Franklin county, near the center of the state. The Ohio Statehouse , found in downtown Columbus, is where the state’s government meets. It has: A large rotunda (a round, domed room), Meeting rooms and chambers for the Ohio Senate and House of Representatives, The Senate Building, which holds more offices and hearing rooms, A big atrium used for public events and rentals, and A gift shop for visitors. The Statehouse is not just a government building—it’s also a historic site and a symbol of Ohio’s democracy. State Nickname Ohio is known as the Buckeye state . People from Ohio are often called Buckeyes , a nickname that dates back to the early 1800s. The name comes from the buckeye tree , which grows across the state. Its nut looks like a deer’s eye—dark brown with a light spot—and early settlers thought it was a good symbol for Ohio. The nickname became popular during William Henry Harrison’s presidential campaign in 1840. His supporters made souvenirs from buckeye wood, helping the name stick. Today, “Buckeye” is used all over Ohio. For example, you'll find it: In place names like Buckeye Lake and the Buckeye Trail , In the n ames of many businesses and organizations , and As the official mascot of The Ohio State University . What started as a simple nickname is now a proud symbol of Ohio’s identity. State-Declared Holidays and Observances The Ohio Legislature can create special days, weeks, or months to raise awareness about important people, events, or causes . These observances are listed in Chapter 5 of the Ohio Revised Code , along with the state’s official symbols. Some examples include: Ohio Statehood Day Breast Cancer Awareness Month Veterans’ Day Ohio Overdose Awareness Day These observances help educate the public and honor Ohio’s history, health, and community. State Animals Bird: Cardinal Adopted: 1953 The cardinal is Ohio’s official state bird. It’s a small songbird that stays in Ohio all year. Cardinals are easy to spot: Males are bright red with a black mask around their faces. Females are brownish-gray with red-orange highlights on their wings, tails, and crests. Both have a sharp crest of feathers on their heads and a bright orange beak. Cardinals eat seeds, fruits, and insects. They are known for being territorial and often mate for life. The state bird is defined in Ohio Revised Code, section 5.06 . Insect: Ladybug Adopted: 1975 The ladybug , also called the ladybird beetle, is Ohio’s official state insect. It’s a small, shiny red bug with black spots, active from spring through fall. Ladybugs are harmless to people but very helpful to farmers and gardeners. They eat aphids and other bugs that damage plants. The most common type in Ohio is the seven-spotted ladybug. It has: A red body, Three black spots on each side, and One black spot in the middle. Their bright colors and bad taste help protect them from predators. Mammal: White-Tailed Deer Adopted: 1988 The white-tailed deer has lived in Ohio since the last Ice Age. It has a gray-brown coat and gets its name from the white underside of its tail, which it raises when alarmed. Native peoples used deer for food, clothing, and tools. Early settlers traded deerskins for supplies, which is how the word “buck” came to mean money. White-tailed deer are foragers. They eat grasses, nuts, berries, wildflowers, crops, and woody plants. Because of their diet, they’re often found near forests and neighborhoods Reptile: Black Racer Snake Adopted: 1995 The black racer lives mostly in the eastern and southern parts of the state. This snake is: Solid black with no markings, Usually 3 to 5 feet long, and Known for being very fast—it can move up to 10 miles per hour! Black racers are helpful to farmers and gardeners because they eat rodents and other small pests. While they can act aggressive if they feel threatened, their bite is not poisonous—just painful. Amphibian: Spotted Salamander Adopted: 2010 The spotted salamander lives in moist woodlands near ponds, swamps, and creeks. These salamanders are: Nocturnal (active at night), Shy burrowers that spend most of their time underground, About 6 to 7.75 inches long, and Able to live up to 20 years. They eat insects, earthworms, small amphibians, and even tiny mice. Because they’re hard to spot, seeing one in the wild is a special treat! Frog: American Bullfrog Adopted: 2010 The bullfrog is the largest frog in North America. It lives in ponds, marshes, and slow-moving streams across the state. Bullfrogs are: Green with brown markings, About 3.5 to 6 inches long, and Known for their deep, loud call, which can be heard up to a mile away! They are solitary and territorial. They eat crayfish, insects, mice, and even other frogs. Bullfrogs can live for 7 to 9 years and are most active from late April through summer. Pet: Shelter Pet Adopted: 2019 Ohio named the shelter pet as its official state pet to help raise awareness about the many cats and dogs waiting for homes in shelters across the state. Each year, about 6.5 million animals enter shelters in the U.S., but only half are adopted. By choosing a shelter pet, you’re giving an animal a second chance at life. To adopt, contact your local animal shelter or humane society and learn how you can help a pet find a loving home. State Plant Life Flower: Red Carnation Adopted: 1953 The scarlet carnation is a colorful plant with fringed petals and a spicy scent. The flower is popular in bouquets and can grow up to 2.5 feet tall. The red carnation stands for love and passion. It was a favorite of President William McKinley, who was born in Ohio and often wore one on his jacket. Tree: Ohio Buckeye Adopted: 1953 The buckeye tree is native to North America. In late summer and early fall, it produces a nut that’s dark brown with a light spot, resembling a deer’s eye—which is how the tree got its name. The nut also inspired the popular chocolate buckeye candy. These treats are made of peanut butter dipped in chocolate, with a bit of the lighter-colored filling left showing to look like the real nut. While the buckeye nut is poisonous, the candy version is safe and delicious Wild Flower: White Trillium Adopted: 1987 The white trillium grows in all 88 Ohio counties and blooms in the spring with a large, white flower made of three petals. Also called the wake robin or snow trillium, this plant grows best in shady woodlands. Native Americans once used its leaves for food and roots for medicine. Fruit: Tomato Adopted: 2009 Many experts credit Alexander W. Livingston , an Ohio native, with creating the modern tomato. In 1870, he developed the “Paragon” tomato , which was larger and sweeter than most tomatoes at the time. Livingston went on to grow tomatoes commercially and created more than 30 varieties. By the late 1800s, tomato farming had become a big part of Ohio’s agriculture—and it still is today. Native Fruit: Pawpaw Adopted: 2009 The pawpaw is the only edible fruit native to Ohio. Native Americans in the Ohio Valley used it for food and trade as early as the 1500s. Pawpaws are: 2 to 4 inches long, Green, yellow, or brown, depending on how ripe they are, and Shaped like a short, fat banana. They taste like a mix of banana and mango and are packed with protein, vitamin C, iron, and potassium. The best time to pick pawpaws is in mid-September. Human-Made State Symbols Beverage: Tomato Juice Adopted: 1965 In 1870, Ohioan Alexander W. Livingston created the modern tomato with his sweet and juicy “Paragon” variety. His tomatoes helped make tomato juice a popular and healthy drink. Tomato juice is: Rich in antioxidants and electrolytes, Lower in sugar than many fruit juices, and Great in soups, sauces, or as a refreshing drink. Due to its popularity, tomatoes and tomato juice are big parts of Ohio’s farming and food industry. Song: "Beautiful Ohio" Adopted: 1989 The music for “Beautiful Ohio” was written by Mary Earl , and the original lyrics were by Ballard MacDonald . In 1989, Wilbert B. McBride updated the lyrics to better reflect Ohio’s cities, industries, and farmland. The song celebrates Ohio’s beauty and strength. Here’s the chorus: Beautiful Ohio, where the golden grain Dwarfs the lovely flowers in the summer rain. Cities rising high, silhouette the sky. Freedom is supreme in this majestic land; Mighty factories seem to hum in tune, so grand. Beautiful Ohio, thy wonders are in view, Land where my dreams all come true! Rock Song: "Hang On Sloopy Adopted: 1985 Ohio is the only state with an official rock song— “Hang on Sloopy.” It became a hit in 1965 when it was recorded by The McCoys , a band with Ohio roots. Two members, Randy and Rick Derringer , were from the state. The song is believed to be about Dorothy Sloo p, a singer from Steubenville, Ohio , who used the nickname Sloopy. The Ohio State University Marching Band first played the song at a football game in October 1965. The version arranged by John Tagenhorst became a fan favorite and is still played at games today. It’s now a proud part of Ohio’s music and sports culture. Bicentennial Bridge: Blaine Hill Bridge Adopted: 2002 The Blaine Hill Bridge is the oldest and longest sandstone bridge in Ohio. It was built in 1826 and crosses Wheeling Creek in Belmont County . The bridge has a unique three-arch “S” shape and was part of the National Road Project , which helped connect the country in the 1800s. It closed to traffic in 1994, but local efforts saved it from being torn down. In 1999, the Blaine Bridge Community Preservation Project began restoring the bridge. It was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2010. Prehistoric Monument: Newark Earthworks Adopted: 2006 Long ago, ancient people in what is now Ohio built huge shapes and structures out of earth. These were made by the Hopewell culture between 1 and 400 A.D. The Newark Earthworks is the largest of these sites. It once covered over 4 square miles and used more than 7 million cubic feet of soil. The site was likely used as a ceremonial center, a burial ground, and even an astronomical observatory. Today, three major parts of the earthworks still remain: The Great Circle , which includes Eagle Mound , The Octagon Earthworks , which align with the moon’s movements, and The Wright Earthworks , a smaller section that shows how the site once looked. These earthworks are a powerful reminder of Ohio’s ancient history and are now protected as a World Heritage Site . Artifact: Adena Pipe Adopted: 2013 The Adena Pipe is one of Ohio’s most famous ancient artifacts. It was found in 1901 in a burial mound near Chillicothe , on the estate of Thomas Worthington , Ohio’s 6th governor. The pipe is carved from Ohio pipestone and shaped like a man wearing a loincloth and feather bustle. It was likely used for ceremonial tobacco smoking and may have belonged to a leader or spiritual figure. The Adena culture , which built the mound, lived in the Scioto and Hocking River valleys from about 800 B.C. to 100 A.D. Historical Architectural Structure: Barn Adopted: 2019 Barns are a big part of Ohio’s farming history. You can find them all over the state—from Lake Erie to the Ohio River. These buildings come in many shapes, sizes, and colors, depending on the needs of the farm and the style of the builder. Some barns were even painted with murals or ads. From 1997 to 2002, artist Scott Hagan painted a barn in each of Ohio’s 88 counties with a special logo to celebrate Ohio’s 200th birthday in 2003 . Barns remind us of Ohio’s strong agricultural roots and the people who helped build its communities. Airplane: 1905 Wright Flyer III Adopted: 2025 In 1905, Ohio inventors Wilbur and Orville Wright built the Wright Flyer III . It was their strongest and most reliable airplane yet. On June 23, 1905, Orville Wright made the first flight with it. By October, the plane flew 25 miles—a huge improvement over earlier flights. It was also the first airplane to carry a passenger, marking a major moment in aviation history. summary: The Auditor of State helps Ohioans report suspected fraud and corruption within state government.

title: Sunshine Laws
summary: Public records and open meeting laws help make Ohio government transparent.
body_html: Ohio's public records and open meetings laws, also known as "Sunshine Laws," create an open government. They help residents observe and take part in government operations and access records.

title: Supreme Court of Ohio
summary: The Supreme Court of Ohio is the highest court in the state.
body_html: The Supreme Court of Ohio is the state's court of last resort. Most of its cases are appeals from the state's district courts of appeals. It is made up of a chief justice and six elected justices. The court is located in the Thomas J. Moyer Ohio Judicial Center in Columbus.

title: Take Charge, Live Well
summary: Take Charge, Live Well is a wellness program for State of Ohio employees and their families.

Program benefits include biometric screenings, health and well-being surveys, health coaching, chronic condition management programs, rewards, and more.
